newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Budapest bucks bear trend on E. Europe bourses.
newsitem.headline: Budapest bucks bear trend on E. Europe bourses.

text.p: A strong dollar and a flow of funds into in Hungarian shares helped the Budapest bourse to buck the bearish tone plaguing most East European markets this week.
Floods depressed Polish and Czech stocks and the tone of the Bratislava and Bucharest bourses was bearish. Blue-chip gains pushed Zagreb and Ljubliana shares higher.
With the exception of Budapest, bourses in the region were unmoved by this week's strong gains on Wall Street.
The Central European Share Index (CESI), which follows price movements in 72 Hungarian, Polish, Czech, Slovak and Slovenian shares, fell to a new 1997 low of 1,405.53 points on Thursday.
BUDAPEST

The Budapest Stock Exchange showed renewed strength this week, mainly on the back of a strong dollar, which made forint-priced shares cheaper for foreigners. The mid-week Dow Jones rally reinforced the trend.
"Conditions are steady -- the dollar is 1.83 (to the mark), the Dow Jones firmed again and there are still floods in (the Czech Republic and Poland)," one trader said.
Market players said funds left the Polish and Czech markets in pursuit of safer investments in Hungary, helping to support price levels.
WARSAW
The Polish share index fell 1.6 percent to 15,102.9 points this week, and analysts said the market should maintain a slight downtrend on macroeconomic concerns into next week.

"Generally the market is slipping the whole time, you can't see demand from foreign investors and you can see there are expectations of an interest-rate rise, especially as money supply is rising," said Czeslaw Pospieszynski of brokers PBI.
Analysts said the heavy flooding had preoccupied the market since it could result in the central bank lending the government up to 2.5 billion zlotys ($723 million).
They also said the run-up to parliamentary elections due on September 21 should also help maintain the mild bearish trend.
PRAGUE

Czech shares traded lower throughout the week, led by the most heavily capitalised banking issue, Komercni Banka, which dealers say has been hit by concerns that flooding in the Czech Republic may eat into profits.
Around one third of the country has been affected by the floods, and Komercni, whose portfolio is dominated by commercial loans, is thought to be more exposed than other banks.
Komercni fell 62 crowns, or 3.8 percent, over the course of the week to close at 1,578 crowns on Thursday, while the PX50 index was 1.01 percent down on the week.
BRATISLAVA
The Bratislava stock exchange extended its sluggish mood, with the official 16-share SAX index dropping 2.65 points, or 1.57 percent over the week.
The SAX fell to a year-low of 164.81 points on Tuesday, but rebounded slightly to close at 166.42 on Thursday.
Brokers said the lacklustre mood of the past few weeks was partly down to a lack of interest among foreign investors.
They said improvements in trading activity should not be expected until local money market liquidity shortages ended, as investors were currently tempted by higher interest rates.
BUCHAREST
Profit-taking was the main feature of the Bucharest exchange during the week, exerting pressure on high-caps and pushing two unofficial indices lower on Thursday.
Traders said some bargain-hunters had emerged on the second-tier but poor liquidity had capped strong gains, keeping the overall market in a bearish mood.
LJUBLJANA
Slovenian shares jumped 5.35 percent this week, with the blue-chip SBI index surging 79.06 points to 1,557.7.

Market participants said the index was set to continue rising over the summer as domestic investors are likely to follow international buyers' activity. The blue-chip index is expected to rise by 30 to 50 percent over the summer.
ZAGREB
Active trading and gains in blue chips Zagrebacka Banka and Pliva drugs company bolstered the Croatian stock market over the week.

Zagrebacka Banka broke through its all-time-high on Thursday and traders said good liquidity might could persist in the short term. Recently-floated ship repairer Viktor Lenac also traded heavily, as did blue chip Varazdinska Banka.
